Empirical Research Plan  
“Does economic growth lead to increases in forest cover in rural India?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Core idea:  exploit plausibly exogenous village-level income shocks generated by the staggered, crop-specific Green Revolution.  

•  First stage (instrument):  Interaction of global HYV-release dates with time-invariant agro-climatic suitability of each village for (i) wheat and (ii) rice.  
•  Second stage (outcome):  Forest cover / biomass (NDVI) within 10-km radius of the village.

Design = Two–stage least squares within a difference-in-differences/event–study framework:

   Forest _vt_ = β Income _vt_  + γ X _vt_  + μ_v  + λ_t  + ε_vt_  
with  

   Income _vt_  (endogenous) ≈ f{Green-Rev Shock_vt_}  

where  

   Green-Rev Shock_vt_  = Wheat_Suit_v  ×  Post-1967_t_  +  Rice_Suit_v  ×  Post-1984_t_

Why appropriate?  
•  HYV release dates were driven by international crop science, not local forestry conditions.  
•  Agronomic suitability is fixed over the sample period.  
•  Staggered timing (wheat first, rice later) yields rich event-time variation that can be visualised in event-study plots and estimated by 2SLS.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable:  Exogenous “income shock” = suitability × post period.

Wheat Module  
•  Treated villages: top tercile of wheat agro-climatic suitability (loamy soils, low humidity, winter temp 15–20 °C, irrigation access ≥25 %).  
•  Control: bottom tercile of wheat suitability.  
•  Treatment timing: 1967 introduction of semi-dwarf wheat. Pretreatment window 1971; post windows 1982, 1991, 1999.

Rice Module  
•  Treated: top tercile of rice suitability (sub-humid tropics, irrigation access, pH 5.5–7.0).  
•  Control: bottom tercile.  
•  Timing: 1984 wide diffusion of IR36/IR64 varieties. Pre = 1971, 1982; post = 1991, 1999.

Combined instrument: both interactions entered simultaneously; income is allowed to respond to both.

No RDD is used; the design is 2SLS-DID/event-study.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Relevance – HYV×Suitability strongly predicts village income/wages.  
Plausible: documented yield boosts of 40–60 % in suitable areas.

A2.  Exclusion – Conditional on fixed effects and controls, HYV×Suitability affects forest only through local economic channels, not via direct forestry policy.  
Plausible: forestry agencies did not allocate protection based on wheat/rice suitability.

A3.  Parallel Trends (reduced form) – In the absence of HYVs, high-suitability and low-suitability villages would have shown similar forest-cover trends.  
Plausible but testable with pre-treatment event-study coefficients (1971 vs. 1982).

A4.  Stable unit treatment (no cross-village fuelwood trade).  
Supported by low value-to-weight of fuelwood and high transport costs.

A5.  Monotonicity – HYV release does not decrease income in any village.  
Reasonable given agronomic evidence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Concurrent forestry reforms (e.g., Joint Forest Management after 1988) targeted to Green-Revolution districts.  
→ Include district-year fixed effects and interact JFM rollout dates with pre-Green-Rev suitability to check for collinearity; run placebo using only pre-1988 years.

T2.  Migration:  HYV areas may attract labor, mechanically changing NDVI through population pressure.  
→ Control for village population; also estimate mechanism regressions where population is the outcome to quantify the channel.

T3.  Differential weather shocks correlating with suitability.  
→ Add village-specific weather controls (growing-season rainfall, degree-days) and interact them with year FE.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (simplified)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
#------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE and 2SLS
library(ggplot2)

#------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
#------------------------------------------
village <- fread("village_panel_1971_1999.csv")   # one row per village-year
soil    <- fread("soil_suitability.csv")           # time-invariant
weather <- fread("village_weather.csv")            # monthly -> annual

data <- merge(village, soil, by="village_id")
data <- merge(data, weather, by=c("village_id","year"))

#------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#------------------------------------------
data[, Post_Wheat := as.integer(year >= 1967)]
data[, Post_Rice  := as.integer(year >= 1984)]

# Suitability indices already in soil file: wheat_suit, rice_suit (0–1)
data[, GR_wheat := wheat_suit * Post_Wheat]
data[, GR_rice  := rice_suit  * Post_Rice ]
data[, GR_shock := GR_wheat + GR_rice]

# Outcomes
data[, ln_ndvi := log(ndvi_10km)]        # NDVI as proxy for biomass
data[, ln_income := log(hh_income_real)]
data[, ln_wage   := log(ag_wage_real)]

#------------------------------------------
# 3. 2SLS estimation with village & year FE
#------------------------------------------
fe_formula <- " | village_id + year"

# First stage
fs <- feols(ln_income ~ GR_wheat + GR_rice + controls + fe_formula, data = data, iv = NULL)

# Second stage (2SLS)
iv <- feols(ln_ndvi ~ 1 | ln_income ~ GR_wheat + GR_rice + controls + fe_formula,
            data = data, cluster = ~district_id)

summary(iv)

#------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study graph (pre-trend test)
#------------------------------------------
# Build relative year to wheat HYV release
data[, rel_year := year - 1967]
event <- feols(ln_ndvi ~ i(rel_year, wheat_suit, ref = -1) + controls | village_id + year,
               data = data[abs(rel_year) <= 15])
iplot(event)        # visual check of pre-coefficients

#------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness:  replace NDVI with Landsat forest-area share
iv_alt <- feols(forest_share ~ 1 | ln_income ~ GR_wheat + GR_rice + controls + fe_formula,
                data = data, cluster = ~district_id)
summary(iv_alt)
```
Notes: “controls” bundles rainfall, degree-days, electrification, roads, and village-specific linear trends where data allow.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory:  Higher rural incomes relax the need to clear forests for cropland, raise demand for cleaner fuels (LPG, electricity), and increase the amenity value of standing forests.  
Prior:  A 10 % increase in village real income should raise NDVI by roughly 0.5 % (β ≈ 0.05). Sign expected: positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (2SLS-DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Relevance of instrument ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion from forest other than via income … 0.8  
C3: Parallel pre-treatment trends …………… 0.9  
C4: No interference/spillovers ……………… 0.7  
C5: Correct functional form & robust SEs …… 1  

Average ≈ 0.88 → design is strong but still vulnerable to spillovers and policy confounds; both are explicitly tested.
